😍Morocco like Pinterest: the most beautiful hotels  🇲🇦  📍 Royal Mansour Marrakech One of the most luxurious hotels in the world, where every guest stays in a private riad with its own courtyard and pool. Carved ceilings, mosaics, and palm gardens. Breakfasts on the terrace and a spa under a glass dome. 📍 El Fenn A place where Morocco meets contemporary art. Bright walls, terracotta rooftop pools, vintage furniture, and rich colors. A bohemian vibe with sunsets overlooking the medina. 📍 La Mamounia A true Marrakech legend. Expansive gardens, arched galleries, emerald tiles, and a pool you’ll want to spend all day in. Classic luxury with history. 📍 Riad Yasmine The iconic Instagram riad with an emerald pool and pink walls. Small, cozy, and incredibly photogenic. Breakfast by the pool with flower petals. 📍 Amanjena Minimalism with Moroccan architecture. Sandy tones, reflective pools, and perfect symmetry. 📍 Kasbah Tamadot A hotel in the Atlas Mountains with views over the valleys. Terraces, Berber style, and warm sunset light. 📍 The Oberoi Marrakech Modern luxury with an oriental touch. Grand pools, arches, reflective water, and clean geometry. 📍 Scarabeo Camp White tents in the Agafay desert. Minimalism, sand dunes, camels, and caramel-colored sunsets. #moroccotravel #luxuryhotels #riadlife #travelinspo #bucketlist

5 things to know before going to Marrakech👇🇲🇦 1️⃣ Moroccan taxis WILL overcharge you, download @inDrive before you arrive. It works at the airport, you set your own price, so there’s no negotiation needed 🚖  2️⃣ Be aware of the animal abuse at Jemaa el-Fnaa. Men walk the square with monkeys in chains and snakes with their teeth removed, don’t pay if they confront you 🙊  3️⃣ Where you stay matters. I found my riad on the @cozycozy app, which compared the prices across all the major booking sites. Agoda was £40 vs £45 on Booking.com, saving £35 over 7 nights 🏨  4️⃣ Eat all the street food. Vendors need licences, so it’s clean, fresh and cheap. I reccoemnd trying this sardine salad just off the main square, search “fried fish” on google maps 🍗  5️⃣ Stay safe in the medina. Wear your backpack on your front, watch out for pickpockets, ignore the men on street corners and download offline maps before you arrive 🎒  Save this video for your trip to Morocco 📌 #marrakech #morocco #jemaaelfna #cozycozy #ad

Spanish Colonialism in Northern Morocco: A History of Occupation, Inequality and Cultural Transformation.  Between 1912 and 1956, Northern Morocco lived under Spanish colonial rule. Behind the beautiful Spanish-influenced architecture, the cafés and the cultural traces that remain today lies a much more complex history — one marked by occupation, power and inequality. The relationship between Spaniards and Moroccans was never simply a story of cultural exchange or peaceful coexistence. It was shaped by a colonial system in which political power, economic resources and social privileges were unequally distributed. Socially, Spaniards and Moroccans shared cities, neighbourhoods, markets and workplaces. Friendships, business relationships and personal connections developed, and some communities lived closely alongside one another. Yet these interactions took place within a hierarchy in which the Spanish colonial authorities held power, while the Moroccan population lived under foreign rule. Economically, colonial development brought roads, ports, infrastructure and new commercial opportunities. But these developments cannot be separated from the interests of the colonial administration. Moroccan labour and resources were part of an economic system largely controlled by Spanish authorities and businesses. Modernisation did not mean equality, nor did it erase economic exploitation. Culturally, Spanish influence became visible in architecture, education, language, food and everyday urban life. But cultural exchange happened under unequal conditions. Moroccan identity, Arabic and Amazigh heritage, religion and traditions continued to shape society, despite the pressures of colonial administration and foreign influence. It is important not to romanticise this period simply because parts of its architectural and cultural legacy are still admired today. Beautiful buildings cannot tell the whole story of colonialism. Behind them were people who experienced occupation, discrimination, political repression and the denial of self-determination. Morocco's history during this period is therefore not just a story of two cultures living side by side. It is also a story of resistance, resilience and the struggle to reclaim independence and national identity. We can acknowledge the cultural influences Spain left behind without forgetting the historical circumstances under which they emerged. Cultural exchange does not justify colonialism, and coexistence does not mean equality. To understand Northern Morocco today, we must look beyond its architecture and recognise the people, inequalities and histories that shaped it. A shared history, but not an equal one.
